• Name: Batman snail (also called Ear snail)
  • Scientific name: Neritina auriculata
  • Water type: freshwater/brackish
  • Minimum tank size: 20 litres (5 gallons)
  • Breeding: difficult
  • Size: 2 cm (0.8 inches) in length
  • KH: 6–16
  • Nitrate: less than 40 ppm
  • Diet: algae eater/detritivore
  • Temperament: peaceful
  • Lifespan: up to 3 years
  • Colour: brownish to olive

Neritina auriculata is a rarity in the US and European pet markets. Information about these snails is scarce and contains some inaccuracies and misconceptions. They are easy to care for and are good cleaners for small aquariums thanks to their preference for algae.

Neritina auriculata occurs widely in the Indo-Pacific region to eastern Africa. Its distribution includes: Japan (Ishigaki Island), Philippines (Negros Island), Indonesia, New Caledonia, Mauritius, French Polynesia, Madagascar, Sri Lanka, Moluccas, New Ireland, Australia, Benin (Porto Novo), Nicobar Islands, Andaman Islands, New Guinea, Solomon Islands, Vanuatu, Fiji, Samoa, New Hebrides, Selornon, Tahiti, Hawaii, Singapore, Guam, Palau, and Yap.

In the wild, Neritina auriculata is usually found in freshwater streams and river estuaries (brackish waters), typically in areas of dense vegetation and algae-covered surfaces (such as stones).

The limited range results from its salinity tolerance and response to hydraulic stress.

Since Batman snails have only been found in streams and rivers, they appear to prefer running water, but they do not like very fast flow. In the Uufau River, the abundance of Neritina auriculata dropped from 114 individuals at water velocities of 0–2 m/s to 6 individuals at velocities above 6 m/s.

Because of their relatively small size, a tank of 20 litres (5 gallons) is suitable for a small group of Batman snails. However, small tanks have potential problems:

  • It can be difficult to keep water parameters stable.
  • It can be hard for the snails to find enough food, causing feeding problems.

Batman snails climb, so use a lid and/or lower the water level.

Batman snails are low-maintenance and easy to care for. They need a well-established tank with stable water parameters, so add them only to a cycled tank. High levels of ammonia and nitrates can be harmful to their health.

They are safe in planted tanks. Although they primarily feed on algae and decaying plant matter, they usually do not consume healthy, live plants, but they may nibble on dying leaves.

Calcium is needed for several vital life processes in snails, the most obvious being the formation of shells.

• Temperature: 22–26°C (72–79°F)
  • pH: 7.0–8.0
  • Hardness: they appreciate hard water, KH above 6 and GH above 12.

Although Neritina auriculata is primarily a freshwater species, in nature these snails are also found in estuarine areas where freshwater and seawater mix. This does not mean they can be placed anywhere. In experiments, snails collected from freshwater habitats and placed in freshwater had a 100% survival rate after 168 hours, but only 60.9–65% survived in seawater over the same period. Snails collected from seawater habitats had a 100% survival rate in seawater and 69% in freshwater after 168 hours.

Snails collected from their natural habitat (either freshwater or seawater) had lower survival rates when placed in the other type of water. Therefore, they require a long adaptation period to be kept long-term in different conditions. Neritina auriculata collected in seawater were also smaller.

Substrate: Batman snails can be kept on any substrate, but smooth gravel is recommended. They do not burrow, so soil or sand substrates are not needed. Their natural environment is composed of small rocks, gravel and boulders, and algae grows more easily on gravel.

Filter: no special requirements, as long as the filter suits the size of the tank.

Decorations: decorations provide shelter and a food source; the more decorations, the greater the surface area for algae, biofilm, etc. to grow. Batman snails cling to rocks, logs and other submerged objects, so they appreciate all types of leaves, rocks, driftwood, PVC pipes, etc.

How to grow algae safely

  • Use a transparent container (a large bottle, spare tank, etc.).
  • Fill it with water taken out during water changes.
  • Add many small clean, aquarium-safe rocks such as marble chips and ceramic filter media.
  • Leave it under the strongest lighting available, ideally 24/7.
  • Use any plant fertilizer.
  • An airstone also boosts algae growth.
  • Once the rocks turn green, take a few and place them in the tank to feed the snails.
  • Return the rocks to the container when they are clean.

These snails are herbivorous and primarily feed on algae. In aquariums they graze on the various algae that grow in the tank, including diatoms (brown algae), green spot algae, green dust algae, biofilm, etc. Like most scavengers, they also consume decaying plant material and organic debris.

They also appreciate blanched vegetables and algae wafers. Because of their small size, it is better to crush the wafer into dust and spread it around the tank.

Batman snails are primarily active at night and often spend the daytime hiding and resting.

They climb surfaces and explore their surroundings, including plants, rocks and driftwood.

They are peaceful and focused on grazing and exploring. Like most snails they are solitary and do not actively seek the company of other snails, but they coexist peacefully with other suitable tank inhabitants. They are not natural diggers; they may unintentionally disturb loose substrate.

  • Social: No
  • Active: At night
  • Peaceful: Yes
  • Burrowers: No

Batman snails are harmless and suit a peaceful community tank, as long as the tankmates have similar water requirements and will not harm or harass the snails.

  • Fish: calm, peaceful fish such as pygmy Cory, clown killifish, least killifish, guppies, peacock gudgeon, harlequin rasboras, Otocinclus, etc.
  • Dwarf shrimp: shrimp that prefer slightly alkaline water are the best choice, e.g. vampire shrimp, bamboo shrimp, Amano shrimp, ghost shrimp, cherry shrimp, blue tiger shrimp, snowball shrimp, Caridina cf. babaulti, blue velvet shrimp, Malawa shrimp, etc.
  • Snails: any freshwater snails, except assassin snails, which easily overpower and eat Batman snails.

Avoid: all types of crayfish (even dwarf Mexican crayfish), most freshwater crabs, and some predatory shrimp such as the Macrobrachium genus (e.g. red claw shrimp, whisker shrimp), all of which can be very aggressive toward the snails. African dwarf frogs are not good tankmates for small Batman snails, as they may try to swallow them.

It is almost impossible to breed Neritina auriculata in captivity; all available snails are wild-caught. Very little is known about their life cycle requirements. According to scientific literature:

  • Batman snails are not hermaphrodites.
  • Females are fertilized internally.
  • Females lay eggs on hard surfaces (such as stones, and even the shells of other snails).
  • Eggs are laid in protective capsules, each containing many eggs.
  • Neritina auriculata has a diadromous life cycle (which is why these snails are never found in stagnant waters). After hatching, larvae cannot thrive in a freshwater aquarium and must be transferred to a brackish setting. Larvae migrate downstream into the marine environment to complete their larval development.

Description: adults typically grow up to 2 cm (0.8 inches) in length, 1.6 cm in width and 0.7 cm in height.

  • Shape: semi-globular shell with a flat base, with 1–1½ whorls; growth lines form semi-circular patterns. The wide opening has two "wings" or "auricles" on the upper and lower sides, hence the name "Batman snail".
  • Aperture: large and half-moon shaped.
  • Operculum: semilunar in shape.
  • Colour: shells are typically brownish to olive with large orange to brown markings. The aperture is yellowish-white and bluish-black around the lip and the columellar area. The operculum has a reddish horn border. The foot is relatively large and oval, usually dark brown.

According to a study, shells in Singapore did not have the large extended "wings" seen on some specimens from Indonesia and Peninsula Malaysia.

Lifespan: the ecology of this species is poorly researched and there is no data on maximum lifespan in the wild. In aquariums they can live at least 2–3 years if appropriately cared for.

Etymology: "Neritina" derives from the Greek "Nerites", a type of sea snail; the name is also used for freshwater snails closely related to marine nerites. In Greek mythology Nerites was the son of Nereus and Doris, who refused the advances of Aphrodite and was turned into a shell. "Auriculata" derives from the Latin "auricula", meaning ear-shaped, referring to the shell.
